name: Solar PV Panel
tagline: Cells in series make the voltage, cells in parallel make the current — the frame carries neither.
terminals: Positive (+) and negative (−) in the junction box
Bypass diodes — one per cell string, inside the box or laminate
Functional earth bond to the module frame
parts: Tempered glass front — 3–4 mm, carries the mechanical load
Encapsulant (EVA) — seals the cells out of the weather
Mono or poly cells — typically 60 or 72, cut into half or third cells
Busbar and finger ribbons — collect current off each cell
Junction box with bypass diodes and MC4 leads
safety: A module in daylight is live and cannot be switched off — Voc sits just above the panel's maximum-power voltage and rises in cold weather. That is why DC isolators, MC4 connectors that can only be separated with a tool, and working on the DC side after dark (or under a cover) are non-negotiable.

points.label: Cell strings
points.detail: Cells are wired in series to build voltage — about 0.6 V per cell, so a 60-cell module gives roughly 36 V at maximum power and nearer 45 V open-circuit when cold. Shade one cell and the whole string current collapses, which is why bypass diodes exist.

points.label: Busbar ribbons
points.detail: Thin tinned copper ribbons run across every cell collecting the current that the hair-like fingers gather off the surface. Modern modules use more, narrower busbars (MBB) to cut resistive loss and to keep output up when a cell cracks.

points.label: Anodised aluminium frame
points.detail: The frame is structural, not electrical — it carries the wind and snow load and gives you somewhere to bolt the clamps. It must still be bonded to earth, because a damaged module can make the frame live.

points.label: Junction box and bypass diodes
points.detail: On the back of the module, holding one diode across each cell string. When a string is shaded the diode conducts around it, so the rest of the panel keeps producing instead of the shaded cells dissipating power as heat — the hotspot that cooks a module.

cutaway.alt: Cutaway of a solar PV panel showing the tempered glass, encapsulant, silicon cells with busbar ribbons, backsheet and frame

cutawayPoints.label: Tempered glass
cutawayPoints.detail: Three to four millimetres, and it is structural: the glass carries the mechanical load, which is why a panel can be walked on by snow and hail and still be sound while the cells inside are only a fraction of a millimetre thick. It is also the layer that has to stay clean, because anything that blocks light blocks current.

cutawayPoints.label: Encapsulant
cutawayPoints.detail: A transparent EVA film that is laminated under vacuum and heat to seal the cells away from moisture. It is the reason a panel survives twenty-five years outdoors — and when it browns or delaminates, moisture reaches the cells and the panel dies from the inside out, usually long before the glass shows a mark.

cutawayPoints.label: Silicon cells
cutawayPoints.detail: The semiconductor that does the work: each cell generates around 0.6 V open circuit regardless of its size, so voltage comes from cells in series and current from cells in parallel. The array is a string of cells, which is why one shaded cell in a series string costs the whole string, not just its own output.

cutawayPoints.label: Busbars and fingers
cutawayPoints.detail: Fine silver fingers collect current across the face of each cell and wider ribbons carry it between cells. They are the panel wiring, and they are thin: thermal cycling and flexing crack them, which is what shows up as hot cells under an infrared survey and a slow, unexplained loss of output.

cutawayPoints.label: Backsheet
cutawayPoints.detail: The insulating rear layer. It is the electrical barrier between the cells and the frame, so damage here — a scrape during installation, a cut from cable ties — is a safety defect, not just cosmetic. Modern panels are often glass on both sides; the insulation requirement does not change.

cutawayPoints.label: Frame
cutawayPoints.detail: Anodised aluminium that carries the mechanical load into the mounting system. The frame is metal and it is touchable, so it gets bonded — the array is a large exposed conductive part, and the frame is where that bonding lands.
